**1. Digest state is cached per thread and replayed to whatever host asks next — `HTTPDigestAuth.__call__` (285–303, especially 289–290), `handle_401` (258–263), `handle_redirect` (236–239)**

Once a nonce is stored, line 289 attaches an `Authorization: Digest` header to every later request made with that same auth object, before any challenge arrives. Nothing binds the cached nonce or challenge to the origin that issued it. `handle_redirect` only resets the 401 counter; it leaves `last_nonce` and `chal` intact. So an auth object reused across hosts, or a redirect chain that ends somewhere else, sends a digest response computed from the user's credentials to a party that never issued the challenge. `handle_401` compounds it: it parses `WWW-Authenticate` from any 4xx responder (258–263) with no check that the responder is the origin the credentials belong to, then re-sends the full request body to that connection (276).

**2. Weak digest parameters accepted with no downgrade protection — `build_digest_header` (138–150, 151–158, 209–216)**

A server that omits `algorithm` gets MD5 (138–139). A captured exchange is then offline-crackable, and the code will also accept SHA-1 (151–158) if offered. Worse, if the server sends no `qop` at all, lines 209–210 fall back to the legacy RFC 2069 response with no client nonce and no nonce count, which is replayable as-is. There is no floor on what the client will agree to; the server picks the weakest option and the client follows. Related, smaller: `qop.split(",")` at 211 doesn't strip whitespace, so `auth-int, auth` misses the `auth` branch and returns `None` at 216, which then gets assigned as a header value at 273–275 and 290.

**3. Basic credentials go out over any scheme, and non-Latin-1 input breaks — `_basic_auth_str` (56–64), `HTTPBasicAuth.__call__` (94–96), `HTTPProxyAuth.__call__` (102–104)**

Nothing here checks the URL scheme. `HTTPBasicAuth` will attach base64 credentials to an `http://` request as readily as `https://`, and base64 is encoding, not protection. The `latin1` encode at 56–60 also raises `UnicodeEncodeError` on any credential outside Latin-1 rather than failing with something a caller can act on, and the deprecation path at 35–53 stringifies arbitrary objects into the header.

**Fix first: #1.** It's the only one where a third party can end up holding a usable credential response without the caller doing anything unusual — reusing one auth object, or following a redirect. The other two need the user to point at a plaintext URL or need the attacker to crack a captured hash. The fix is also contained: key the cached nonce and challenge to the origin that issued them, and clear both in `handle_redirect` when the host changes.
